question.text: A pension fund manager wants to increase the portfolio's interest rate sensitivity (duration) without purchasing additional bonds. Which IRF strategy achieves this?

answer.text: Buy (long) 13-year GOI bond futures, as the long futures position adds duration to the portfolio
Sell 13-year GOI bond futures to increase duration
Buy 91-day T-Bill futures for maximum duration addition
Sell MIBOR futures to increase the portfolio's yield sensitivity

explanation.text: The Logic: A long bond futures position synthetically adds duration to the portfolio. By buying 13-year GOI bond futures, the pension fund increases its interest rate sensitivity without tying up capital in physical bonds. The longer the tenor, the more duration is added per lot. The Trap: Selling futures would reduce (not increase) duration. 91-day T-Bill futures add minimal duration due to their short tenor. MIBOR futures hedge overnight rates and don't add meaningful duration. Cross-Exam Context: Duration management using futures is a key concept for institutional portfolio management, tested in NISM Series IV. Synthetic duration adjustment is capital-efficient compared to physical bond purchases. Distributor's Pro-Tip: This is called 'duration overlay' — using futures to adjust portfolio duration above or below the physical bond portfolio's duration. It's especially useful for pension funds that need to maintain high duration to match long-dated liabilities but have limited new capital to deploy.
